title: When buyers ask AI for "best X", vendors get 2% of citations
content:
What the data says
- When a buyer asks "best X for Y", vendors get 2% of citations. The other 98% goes to third parties — mostly listicles, YouTube, and other vendors' blogs.
- When a user asks a specific factual question, vendors get 43–57%. The questions you can win are the ones asked by people who already found you.
- Reddit was 0.35% of all citations — and every single one came from Gemini. The ChatGPT and Perplexity APIs cited Reddit zero times in 810 answers. G2, Capterra and TrustRadius combined: 0–3%.
- The #1 non-vendor source is YouTube. The #2 is Zapier's blog — cited 93 times in answers about Zapier's competitors.
- Each engine has its own source diet. 92% of TechRadar citations came from ChatGPT. 65% of YouTube citations came from Perplexity. Which engine your buyers use changes which sources matter.
- AI engines don't trash established brands. 742 brand mentions, zero warnings. What varies — from 10% to 80% — is whether you're framed as the answer or just an answer.
01Two kinds of questions, two different games
Every question a user asks an AI assistant about software falls into one of two shapes, and the engines treat them almost as different products.
Discovery questions — "best CRM for a small agency", "Notion vs Asana" — ask the engine to rank or choose. Technical questions — "does HubSpot have email sequences", "how do I set up Klaviyo flows", "is Typeform free" — ask it to verify a fact about a product the user can already name.
Here is who gets cited, across 810 answers:
Vendor share of cited sources, by question type
Share of all citation URLs resolving to the vendor's own domain (including docs.*, help.*, developer.*)
The split is not subtle, and it is not about content quality. These are 27 companies with excellent websites — Stripe, Notion, Figma, HubSpot, Slack, Canva. When the question has a precise factual answer, engines go to the source: the vendor's own pages carry 43–57% of citations, and on how-to questions roughly a fifth of those vendor citations land on docs.* and help.* subdomains specifically.
The mechanism behind the gap is more mundane than it looks, and worth stating plainly: an AI assistant answering a question runs a search, reads the top handful of results, and writes from those. When someone names your product, the search is your brand name — your site ranks first, gets read, gets cited. When someone asks for "the best CRM for agencies", the search is that phrase, and your product page does not rank for it. Round-ups do. The engine never sees your site, so it cannot cite it. There is no judgment being made about vendor bias; you simply aren't in the reading pile.
The questions your website can win are the ones asked by people who already know you exist. The questions that create new customers are decided on pages you don't control.
02Three things everyone believes that the citations don't support
Reddit accounted for 22 of 6,375 citations — 0.35%. More striking than the size is the distribution: all 22 came from Gemini. The ChatGPT and Perplexity APIs cited Reddit zero times across all 810 answers.
One caveat we'll make for you before you make it: consumer ChatGPT, which has a content deal with Reddit, visibly surfaces Reddit threads in its app. Our probes ran against the APIs. If your buyers use the consumer apps, Reddit may matter more than this shows — but in the retrieval layer we could measure, it is close to absent, and two of three engines never touched it.
G2, Capterra and TrustRadius combined accounted for 0–3% of citations per question type. For a category of sites whose entire pitch is being the trusted aggregation layer, they are strikingly absent from the answer layer.
Part of this may be self-inflicted. When we ran our own crawler over these sites, g2.com's homepage was blocked by bot protection — the same class of defence that stops AI fetchers reading a page. Review aggregators may be under-cited partly because they've made themselves hard to read. Their scores may still matter indirectly, as inputs to the listicles that do get cited.
True only for the questions where you're named. On category and comparison questions, roughly nine out of ten citations go to third parties. Your site's job on those questions is not to be the answer — it's to be accurately represented in the pages that are.
03Who actually wins the discovery questions
If vendors get 2%, who gets the rest? We tallied every host cited on category and comparison questions. The leaderboard is not what the marketing playbooks predict.
Most-cited non-vendor hosts — category + comparison questions
Number of citations across all three engines. Green = another SaaS vendor's content marketing.
Three things stand out.
YouTube is the single biggest citation target. Video reviews and walkthrough content out-cite every text publication. Almost no SaaS content strategy treats YouTube as an AI-visibility channel.
The second-biggest source is a competitor. Zapier's blog was cited 93 times — overwhelmingly in answers about other companies' categories. Monday.com, HubSpot and Salesforce show the same pattern at smaller scale. Zapier obviously publishes that content deliberately; what almost nobody does is treat it as an AI-citation strategy and measure it as one.
The rest is the listicle economy — TechRadar, Forbes, and mid-size specialist reviewers like The Digital Project Manager and EmailToolTester. If your brand isn't in the round-ups these engines keep citing, you are not a candidate answer on discovery questions, regardless of how good your product page is.
Except "the engines" is the wrong unit
Aggregating three engines into one leaderboard hides the most practical finding in the dataset. Split the same citations by which engine produced them:
Same hosts, split by engine
Category + comparison citations. The aggregate leaderboard is mostly an average of three very different habits.
"YouTube is the top source" is really Perplexity's top source — 65% of those citations are Perplexity's. The listicle economy is largely ChatGPT's house style: 92% of TechRadar citations and 74% of Forbes citations came from ChatGPT alone. And every Reddit citation in the study came from Gemini.
Which means the practical advice depends on which engine your buyers use. If they're in Perplexity, video coverage is the lever. If they're in ChatGPT, it's the big tech round-ups. The one source that pays across all three is other vendors' blogs — Zapier's citations split almost evenly between Perplexity and Gemini, and it's the only host in the top five that isn't dominated by a single engine.
04The engines are not talking trash about anyone
We also classified the tone of all 742 brand mentions the engines produced: is the brand framed as the leader, mentioned neutrally, hedged with a caveat, or warned against?
Zero warnings in 742 mentions. For established SaaS, the fear that AI assistants are out there bad-mouthing your product is unsupported — the worst that happens is a mild caveat, and even the most-hedged brand in the sample (Figma, at 17% caveats) is hedged less than one time in five.
What varies enormously is the leader framing. Typeform was presented as a top choice in 80% of its mentions; Figma in 10%. That spread doesn't track website quality, size, or product excellence — Figma's product is not worse than Typeform's. It tracks how tightly the training corpus binds the brand to a specific use case. "Typeform" means elegant forms in the corpus; "Figma" shares its category with a decade of design-tool discourse. That association was built over years of third-party writing, and no on-site change moves it quickly.
05The strangest result: famous, discussed, never cited
One brand produced the study's cleanest anomaly. Notion was mentioned in 100% of its answers — and its website was cited in 0% of them. The engines know Notion the way people know Coca-Cola: as common knowledge that needs no reference. When they discuss it, they cite listicles about Notion rather

report.summary: An 810-answer study finds vendor sites win only 2% of AI citations on 'best X' discovery questions, while YouTube, listicles and rivals' blogs dominate.
report.background: As buyers increasingly ask ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini which product to buy, being cited inside those answers has become the new organic search ranking. A whole discipline — generative engine optimisation, or GEO — has grown up around the assumption that vendors can win these citations with good content. This study tested that assumption directly by running 810 software-buying questions through three engines and resolving 6,375 cited sources back to their hosts. The results cut against most marketing playbooks: AI assistants retrieve and read the top search results, so whoever ranks for the query gets cited, not whoever has the best product page. The findings matter because more purchase research now starts and ends inside an assistant answer, with fewer clicks through to vendor sites.
key_points: Vendor sites capture only about 2% of citations on discovery questions like 'best CRM for agencies', but 43–57% on specific factual and how-to questions. The rule: you win the questions asked by people who already know your name, and lose the ones that create new customers.

YouTube is the single largest non-vendor citation source on category and comparison questions, followed by Zapier's blog — a competitor's content marketing, cited 93 times mostly in answers about Zapier's rivals. The rest is the listicle economy: TechRadar, Forbes and specialist reviewers.

Each engine has its own source diet, so the aggregate leaderboard is misleading. 92% of TechRadar citations came from ChatGPT, 65% of YouTube citations from Perplexity, and every single Reddit citation in the study came from Gemini — ChatGPT and Perplexity APIs cited Reddit zero times.

Review aggregators barely register: G2, Capterra and TrustRadius combined account for 0–3% of citations. Some of that may be self-inflicted, since such sites deploy bot protection that blocks AI fetchers from reading their pages in the first place.

AI engines do not disparage established brands — 742 brand mentions produced zero warnings. What varies hugely is framing: Typeform was presented as a top choice in 80% of mentions, Figma in only 10%, tracking how tightly the corpus binds a brand to a use case. Notion was mentioned in 100% of its answers but cited 0% of the time, treated as common knowledge needing no source.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes retrieval as the real battleground: assistants are only as vendor-friendly as the search layer beneath them, and whoever controls ranking controls citations. For developers and SaaS marketers, the practical takeaway is that on-site content and product pages cannot win discovery queries — presence in third-party round-ups, video reviews and even competitors' blogs does. Measurement should shift from traffic to share-of-answer, and split by engine rather than averaged. For regular users, the upside is that answers are mostly sourced from independent reviews, not vendor copy, and established brands are rarely bad-mouthed. The risk is a homogenised listicle economy feeding every recommendation, with paywalled or bot-blocked review sites squeezed out entirely.
report.tools: To follow up, try AI-visibility trackers such as Profound, Otterly.ai, Peec AI, AthenaHQ, Scrunch and Semrush's AI toolkit, which log brand mentions and citations across engines. For do-it-yourself audits, query the OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Perplexity APIs directly and parse returned citations, as this study did. Exa and Tavily expose retrieval-layer results, useful for seeing which pages an assistant would actually read, and Cloudflare's bot-management logs reveal whether AI crawlers can reach your site at all.
